title: Path traversal in export_to_json allows arbitrary file write to any location on disk
description: The CADDataConverter.export_to_json() method writes extraction results to an output_path supplied by the caller with no path validation or sanitization. An attacker who controls the output_path parameter can write arbitrary JSON content to any location writable by the process, including overwriting configuration files, cron jobs, or SSH authorized_keys.
impact: Arbitrary file write leading to potential remote code execution. An attacker can overwrite sensitive system files (e.g., ~/.bashrc, cron entries, web server configs) or plant webshells in document roots.
attack_path: 1. Attacker provides a crafted output_path such as '../../../../etc/cron.d/backdoor' or '../../../var/www/html/shell.php'
2. The export_to_json() method at line 542-551 calls open(output_path, 'w') without any path validation
3. json.dump(output, f, indent=2) writes attacker-influenced content to the arbitrary path
4. If written to a cron directory or web-accessible location, attacker gains code execution

evidence.snippet: def export_to_json(self, result: CADExtractionResult, output_path: str):

remediation: Validate and sanitize output_path before writing: resolve the real path with os.path.realpath(), ensure it falls within an allowed output directory using os.path.commonpath(), reject paths containing '..' components, and enforce an allowlist of permitted output directories.

title: Path traversal via crafted PDF filename in batch_extract_tables enables arbitrary file write
description: The batch_extract_tables() function constructs output filenames from the PDF file's stem name (pdf_path.stem) without sanitization and writes to a user-controlled output_folder. A PDF file named '../../etc/cron.d/evil.pdf' would produce an output path like '<output_folder>/../../etc/cron.d/evil_p1_t1.xlsx', escaping the intended output directory. Additionally, both folder_path and output_folder parameters accept arbitrary paths with no validation.
impact: Arbitrary file write to locations outside the intended output directory. An attacker who can place a maliciously-named PDF in the input folder (or control folder_path) can write Excel files to arbitrary filesystem locations, potentially overwriting critical files.
attack_path: 1. Attacker places a PDF with a traversal name like '../../tmp/evil.pdf' in the input folder, or controls folder_path to read from an arbitrary directory
2. batch_extract_tables() at line 347 globs *.pdf files and iterates them
3. At line 361, output_name is constructed as f"{pdf_path.stem}_p{page_num+1}_t{table_num+1}.xlsx" using the unsanitized stem
4. At line 362, the file is written to Path(output_folder) / output_name, which resolves the traversal components
5. Extracted data is written to an attacker-controlled filesystem location
remediation: Sanitize the PDF filename stem by stripping or rejecting path separator characters and '..' components. Use os.path.basename() on the stem, validate output_folder resolves within an allowed directory, and verify the final resolved output path stays within the output_folder boundary.

title: Piped curl-to-shell installation command enables remote code execution via MITM or DNS hijack
description: The SKILL.md instructs users to install Ollama by piping curl output directly to a shell: 'curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh'. This is a well-known insecure pattern. If an attacker can perform a man-in-the-middle attack, compromise DNS resolution, or if the remote server is compromised, arbitrary shell commands will be executed with the user's privileges without any integrity verification.
impact: Remote code execution with the privileges of the user running the command. A compromised download yields full system compromise since the script is executed immediately without signature verification or checksum validation.
attack_path: 1. User follows the installation instructions at line 224
2. curl fetches https://ollama.com/install.sh - if TLS is downgraded, DNS is poisoned, or the server is compromised, a malicious script is served
3. The -s flag suppresses curl errors, -f still passes content to sh on certain failure modes
4. sh executes whatever is downloaded, running arbitrary commands with user privileges
5. Attacker achieves code execution, can install backdoors, steal credentials, or pivot
remediation: Download the script first, verify its checksum/signature, review its contents, then execute: 'curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh -o install.sh && sha256sum install.sh && sh install.sh'. Alternatively, use the platform's package manager or provide a verified binary download with checksum.

title: Arbitrary file read via unsanitized PDF path in analyze_pdf_drawing allows reading sensitive files
description: The DrawingAnalyzer.analyze_pdf_drawing() method opens a PDF file from a user-supplied path with no validation. If this function is exposed through an API or web interface, an attacker can supply paths like '/etc/passwd', '/proc/self/environ', or application configuration files to exfiltrate sensitive data through the extracted text and metadata returned in DrawingAnalysisResult.
impact: Arbitrary file read leading to information disclosure. An attacker can read application secrets, configuration files, environment variables, and other sensitive data from the server filesystem.
attack_path: 1. Attacker provides a crafted pdf_path such as '/etc/shadow', '../../../app/config/database.yml', or '/proc/self/environ'
2. analyze_pdf_drawing() at line 108 passes the unsanitized path to Path(pdf_path)
3. At line 118, pdfplumber.open(pdf_path) attempts to open the file
4. If the file is a valid PDF or if pdfplumber's error contains file content hints, data is extracted
5. Text content is returned in DrawingAnalysisResult.title_block, dimensions, and annotations fields
remediation: Validate that pdf_path resolves to a location within an allowed directory. Use os.path.realpath() to resolve symlinks, then check that the resolved path starts with the configured allowed base directory. Reject absolute paths and paths containing '..' components.

title: Arbitrary file read via unsanitized image paths in analyze_image and compare_to_bim
description: ConstructionProgressAnalyzer.analyze_image() opens arbitrary files via Image.open(image_path) with no path validation. Similarly, compare_to_bim() opens two user-controlled file paths using cv2.imread(). An attacker controlling these paths can read arbitrary files from the filesystem. Even if the file is not a valid image, error messages or partial reads may leak file contents or confirm file existence.
impact: Arbitrary file read and file existence oracle. An attacker can probe the filesystem structure and read files accessible to the process, potentially exfiltrating secrets, source code, or configuration.
attack_path: 1. Attacker supplies image_path as '/etc/passwd' or '/app/.env' to analyze_image()
2. At line 119, Image.open(image_path) attempts to open and read the file
3. For compare_to_bim(), at lines 281-282, cv2.imread() reads two arbitrary paths
4. Even on failure, exception messages reveal whether files exist and may leak partial content
5. If the file happens to be parseable as an image format, pixel data may encode file contents
remediation: Validate file paths against an allowlist of permitted directories. Use os.path.realpath() to resolve the path, then verify it falls within the expected uploads or data directory. Reject paths with '..' components, and ensure only expected image file extensions are accepted.

title: Arbitrary file write via unsanitized output paths in export_model and export_to_excel
description: MLModelBuilder.export_model() writes model JSON data to a user-controlled output_path using open(output_path, 'w') with no path validation. Similarly, export_to_excel() writes to a user-controlled output_path. An attacker who controls these parameters can write files to arbitrary locations on the filesystem, potentially overwriting critical configuration files or planting malicious content.
impact: Arbitrary file write that can overwrite application configuration, inject code into startup scripts, or plant files in web-accessible directories for further exploitation.
attack_path: 1. Attacker calls export_model() with output_path set to '../../../../root/.ssh/authorized_keys' or similar sensitive path
2. At line 401, open(output_path, 'w') opens the file for writing without any path validation
3. At line 402, json.dump() writes model data (which includes attacker-influenced field values from training data) to the file
4. The target file is overwritten or created with attacker-influenced content
5. For export_to_excel() at line 409, pd.ExcelWriter(output_path) similarly writes to an arbitrary path

evidence.snippet: def export_model(self, model_id: str, output_path: str) -> str:

remediation: Validate output_path by resolving it with os.path.realpath() and confirming it resides within an expected output directory. Reject any path containing '..' traversal sequences. Use a dedicated output directory with restricted permissions.

title: API key leaked in URL query parameters, exposable in server logs, proxies, and browser history
description: The OpenPriceAPI class sends the FRED API key as a URL query parameter (params['api_key']) rather than in an HTTP header. URL query parameters are routinely logged by web servers, proxies, CDNs, and browser history. This exposes the API key to any system that logs or caches request URLs.
impact: API key disclosure leading to unauthorized API usage, quota exhaustion, and potential cost to the key owner. If the same key is reused across services, lateral access to other APIs becomes possible.
attack_path: 1. Application calls get_fred_prices() which constructs request with api_key in URL params at line 100
2. requests.get() sends the request to FRED API with the key visible in the URL query string
3. Intermediate proxies, load balancers, WAFs, or logging systems record the full URL including the API key
4. An attacker with access to log files, proxy caches, or network captures extracts the API key
5. Attacker uses the stolen key to make unauthorized API calls or exhaust rate limits
remediation: Note: The FRED API specifically requires the key as a query parameter, so this is partly an upstream API design issue. Mitigate by: using environment variables to store the key (never hardcoding), ensuring logging infrastructure redacts query parameters containing 'api_key', using HTTPS exclusively, and rotating keys regularly. Document the exposure risk for users.

title: Multiple functions accept unsanitized file paths enabling arbitrary file read from the filesystem
description: Several functions in the pdf-to-structured skill accept user-controlled file paths that are passed directly to pdfplumber.open() and file write operations without any path validation: extract_tables_from_pdf(pdf_path), extract_text_with_layout(pdf_path), extract_table_from_area(pdf_path, ...), ocr_scanned_pdf(pdf_path), and parse_specification_pdf(pdf_path). Additionally, extract_text_with_layout() writes extracted content to a hardcoded text file, and export_to_multiple_formats() writes to user-controlled base_name paths.
impact: Arbitrary file read from the filesystem when any of these functions are exposed through a web interface or API. An attacker can read any PDF-parseable file, and through the export functions, write extracted content to arbitrary locations.
attack_path: 1. Attacker supplies a crafted pdf_path containing path traversal sequences like '../../../sensitive/data.pdf'
2. Functions at lines 62, 91, 115, 147, 304 pass the path directly to pdfplumber.open()
3. pdfplumber reads the file and extracts text/tables from it
4. Extracted content is returned to the caller, exposing sensitive document contents
5. export_to_multiple_formats() at line 417 writes to user-controlled base_name enabling arbitrary file write
remediation: Implement a path validation utility that all file-accepting functions use: resolve real paths, enforce that they reside within an allowed base directory, reject '..' sequences and absolute paths, and validate file extensions match expected types (e.g., .pdf for PDF functions).

title: Unsanitized file path in extract_from_pdf enables arbitrary PDF file read
description: SpecificationExtractor.extract_from_pdf() accepts a user-supplied pdf_path and passes it directly to pdfplumber.open() with no path validation. When exposed through an API, this allows reading arbitrary PDF files from the filesystem and returning their parsed content (sections, products, submittals, standards) through the SpecExtractionResult.
impact: Information disclosure through arbitrary file read. Sensitive PDF documents outside the intended scope (contracts, financial documents, HR records) can be read and their structured content extracted and returned to the attacker.
attack_path: 1. Attacker provides a path like '/app/private/contracts/confidential.pdf' or '../../secrets/internal_report.pdf'
2. extract_from_pdf() at line 103 passes the path to pdfplumber.open(pdf_path) at line 110
3. The full text is extracted and parsed into sections, products, submittals, and standards
4. The structured SpecExtractionResult containing sensitive document content is returned to the attacker
remediation: Validate pdf_path by resolving it to a real path and checking it resides within an allowed documents directory. Reject paths with '..' components and validate the file extension is .pdf.

title: API key hardcoded in example usage encourages insecure credential handling
description: The Quick Start section demonstrates initializing the API client with a plaintext string 'your_key' as the API key parameter. While this is a placeholder, the pattern encourages hardcoding credentials directly in source code. No guidance is provided for using environment variables, secret managers, or configuration files. Combined with the key being sent as a URL parameter (VULN-007), this creates a credential exposure chain.
impact: Developers copying this pattern will hardcode API keys in source files, which get committed to version control, shared in logs, and exposed in CI/CD pipelines, leading to credential leakage.
attack_path: 1. Developer follows the Quick Start example and replaces 'your_key' with their actual FRED API key in source code
2. The file is committed to a Git repository (potentially public)
3. An attacker scanning public repositories finds the hardcoded API key
4. Attacker uses the key for unauthorized API access
remediation: Update examples to use environment variables: api = OpenPriceAPI(fred_api_key=os.environ.get('FRED_API_KEY')). Add a note warning against hardcoding credentials and recommend using .env files excluded from version control.
